name: Sending Off (The Ordinary Version)
description:
No one knows exactly when 'Sending Off (The Ordinary Version)' first appeared. It exists in no official catalog. It has no registered composer. The earliest confirmed recording dates to approximately 2191, but oral accounts from Shelf elders place variants of the melody as far back as 2175, passed between communities in the lower wards as a sung farewell for the dead. The title's parenthetical — 'The Ordinary Version' — is understood to be an act of defiance: a statement that the deaths of ordinary people deserve a ceremony as real and permanent as any Spire memorial. The song is structured as a slow, cyclical melody built on a Middle Eastern maqam scale interwoven with West African communal call-and-response, and it is almost always performed live, a cappella, by whoever is present. There is no canonical recording. Every performance is the real version.

The lyrics — which vary by community but share a stable core — speak directly to the dead person, telling them specific small things: the name of their street, the color of their door, what the light looked like from their window. The practice of inserting personal details into the stable melodic structure means every performance is simultaneously the same song and entirely unique. It is sung at Shelf funerals, at memorials for workers killed in industrial accidents, at vigils for those who disappeared into corporate detention. It has been sung, quietly and illegally, inside at least two Vantablack Media holding facilities.
creator: traditional (Shelf oral tradition, origin unattributed)
genre: Shelf Traditional, A Cappella Communal, Funeral Folk, Maqam-West African Fusion
audience: Shelf and Circuit communities, primarily at funerals, vigils, and memorials; any community gathering to grieve collectively
cultural_impact: The song has become the de facto funeral standard for the lower tiers of GLMZ, filling the role that formal religious or state ceremony does not adequately serve for Shelf residents who have neither the resources for elaborate ritual nor the institutional support of organizations that recognize their dead. Its existence as an unregistered, unowned, communally-held piece of music has made it legally and commercially untouchable — there is nothing for a corporation to acquire or suppress. Musicologists from Tier 3 universities have attempted to document and formalize it; their papers are generally received in the Shelf with polite hostility.
known_fans: labor unions (sung at deaths of members)
religious and secular grief communities in the lower wards
story_hooks: A Tier 3 musicologist has produced a definitive academic recording of the song and is seeking to register it with a cultural heritage organization — an act that the Shelf community views as an act of theft regardless of the scholar's intentions.

A player character attends a Shelf funeral and hears the song sung for someone they are later told was a corporate informant — and the community's grief is entirely genuine, which complicates everything.

The song is reportedly being sung inside a Vantablack Media detention facility by a group of labor organizers being held without formal charges, and a journalist has audio evidence — but publishing it would reveal the source.
